newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel's Netanyahu has talks with Egypt's Mubarak.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu has talks with Egypt's Mubarak.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Cairo on Wednesday to a barrage of hostility from the Egyptian press, angered by his latest decisions on Arab East Jerusalem.
He went straight into talks with President Hosni Mubarak, who has said he will tell Netanyahu of the dire consequences of Israel's plan to build more houses for Jews in the city.

Netanyahu, on his second visit to the largest Arab state and the first to make peace with the Jewish state, raised the stakes on Tuesday by ordering four Palestinian offices to close in the disputed sector of Jerusalem.
The Egyptian judiciary threw another spanner into the works when it set a trial date of April 24 for Azam Azam, an Israeli accused of spying in Egypt for the Israeli secret service Mossad.

Mubarak had wanted to take the opportunity to spell out Arab concerns over the rate of progress towards Middle East peace, especially after Netanyahu decided last week to go ahead with the housing for 6,500 Jews in the Jabal Abu Ghneim quarter.
But Netanyahu said late on Tuesday that he wanted to talk most of all about the case of Azam.

"Azam Azam is at the top of my agenda...He has been jailed on a false charge of espionage, or assisting in espionage for Israel. He is not an agent of any of the Israeli intelligence organs - I can guarantee that. He is not an indirect agent."
"He is nothing as far as Israeli intelligence is concerned. He is an Israeli citizen who has been falsely accused and we want him out," he said.
Mubarak is likely to give him short shrift on that point. He has repeatedly said that once Israel publicised the case he could not interfere in the judicial process.
To Egyptian public opinion, releasing Azam now would look like a gratuitous concession to an unpopular foreign leader.
Egyptian newspapers on Wednesday, even those owned by the state, reflected the sour mood in relations.
The government newspaper al-Akhbar showed the Israeli prime minister stuck at a roadblock on the outskirts of Cairo in a limousine. "No Entry", says the road sign.
The opposition newspaper al-Wafd showed scores of workers spraying the airport tarmac with disinfectant as Netanyahu's plane lands. "It's because that guy arrives," says one.
The cartoon was partly a pun on Netanyahu's name, the first two syllables of which mean rotten or putrid in Arabic.
An editorial in al-Akhbar said that Netanyahu, with his decision on Jerusalem housing, had reinforced Cairo's suspicions that he is not serious about Middle East peace.
"Netanyahu's policies have convinced the Egyptian people and the Arab peoples that Israel is proceeding in the peace process against its will," it said.
"How can we Arabs deal with trust and in a normal manner with such people, who smile and laugh whenever peace runs into a crisis?" it added.
Broad sectors of Egyptian public opinion oppose the very concept of a visit by Netanyahu and al-Akhbar said even those in government would look askance at his presence.

"Would it not be better for Mr Netanyahu to feel that Egyptians are welcoming him...instead of seeing angry looks in the eyes of all, even if they have to accept his presence merely as an official guest?" it asked.
After talks with Mubarak, Netanyahu is scheduled to hold a news conference and then have lunch with the president.
In the afternoon he is due to have meetings with Egyptian and Israeli business people and then with Egyptian editors. He is scheduled to fly home in the early evening.
